screens: Plan your first step Practice: not part of your experiment. What happensRate how starting feels.Write a short when-then plan and read it twice.Rate again.About 3 minutes. Nothing you write or choose is saved. Only that you did this exercise, and when, is kept on this computer. You can stop at any time.Why this exercise?The science behind it: Implementation intentions What you doYou write down what you want to start, when you'll start, a tiny first step, and what you'll do if something gets in the way. Then you read your plan twice. The method: If-then planning (implementation intentions)Instead of only deciding what you want to do, you link a specific moment to a specific action: “When it's 7 pm and I'm at my desk, I'll open chapter 3.” The idea is that the moment itself then prompts you, so starting needs less deciding on the spot. What research says about this methodResearch found that people who made if-then plans reached their goals more often than people who only set the goal, across 94 experiments. Gollwitzer & Sheeran, 2006 Full text checkedA larger review of 642 experiments found that, after allowing for experiments that were never published, the benefit is small. It was larger when people strongly wanted the goal, and close to zero when they didn't. Sheeran, Listrom & Gollwitzer, 2025 Full text checked About this exerciseThis exercise follows the if-then planning method, but this version hasn't been tested itself. The research above tested if-then plans in its own forms and settings, not in this app. LimitsExpect a small effect at most, and only for goals you genuinely want.Effects were smaller online and in everyday settings than in the lab. Sources Gollwitzer & Sheeran, 2006. Implementation intentions and goal achievement: A meta-analysis of effects and processes. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 38, 69–119 (opens in a new tab) Sheeran, Listrom & Gollwitzer, 2025. The when and how of planning: Meta-analysis of the scope and components of implementation intentions in 642 tests. European Review of Social Psychology, 36(1), 162–194 (opens in a new tab)BeginBack

The method: Stating your goal (the comparison exercise)Research on if-then planning compares people who make a plan with people who only state their goal. What research says about this methodResearch found that adding an if-then plan led to more goal progress than stating the goal alone. Stating the goal was the point of comparison in that research, not a method tested on its own. Picture it, then follow the dot Practice: not part of your experiment. What happensRate how starting feels.Choose a picture, try the game, then play 8 short rounds while holding the picture.Plan your first step.Rate again.About 10 minutes. Nothing you write or choose is saved. Only that you did this exercise, and when, is kept on this computer. You can stop at any time.Why this exercise?The science behind it: Working-memory taxation What you doYou hold a picture of something you feel stuck on in mind while following a moving dot for 8 short rounds, then plan your first step. The method: Holding a picture in mind during a demanding task (working-memory taxation)Working-memory taxation involves deliberately placing demands on working memory, the limited mental resources we use to hold and process information in the moment. Researchers use this approach in different ways to investigate cognitive processes such as working-memory performance, attention and mental imagery.In this exercise, the technique is used for a specific purpose: you hold a negative mental image in mind while tracking a moving target. Because both tasks compete for limited cognitive resources, the image may become less vivid and its associated emotional intensity may decrease temporarily.This is one application of the broader approach, not the only purpose of working-memory taxation. What research says about this methodA lab experiment with 37 students found that recalling a recurring, unpleasant image of a feared future event during an eye-movement task made it less vivid straight afterwards than recall alone. The drop in how upsetting it felt was smaller and unclear. Engelhard et al., 2011 Full text checkedThe kind of task matters: in two lab experiments, a visual game played after a distressing film reduced later intrusive images; a word quiz did not, and once increased them. Holmes, James, Kilford & Deeprose, 2010 Full text checked About this exerciseThis is an experimental exercise, and this version hasn't been tested itself. The lab experiment used eye movements, not a moving dot. The planning step uses the method of “Plan your first step”. LimitsEffects were modest and immediate; how long they last is unknown.It hasn't been shown that a less vivid picture helps anyone start.Choose an everyday situation, never a painful personal memory. Sources Engelhard et al., 2011. Reducing vividness and emotional intensity of recurrent “flashforwards” by taxing working memory: An analogue study. Journal of Anxiety Disorders, 25, 599–603 (opens in a new tab) Holmes, James, Kilford & Deeprose, 2010. Key steps in developing a cognitive vaccine against traumatic flashbacks: Visuospatial Tetris versus verbal Pub Quiz. PLoS ONE, 5(11), e13706 (opens in a new tab)BeginBack

Nothing you write or choose is saved. Only that you did this exercise, and when, is kept on this computer. You can stop at any time.Why this exercise?The science behind it: Distraction What you doYou follow a moving dot for 8 short rounds without holding any picture in mind. Afterwards you plan your first step. The method: A short, focused game (the comparison exercise)This is the same game as “Picture it, then follow the dot”, with the same rounds and pauses, but without the picture. Comparing the two shows whether holding the picture adds anything beyond a short break or a distraction. What research says about this methodResearch suggests that turning your attention to something else can ease difficult feelings for a while: a review of emotion-regulation experiments reported a small benefit of distraction. Webb, Miles & Sheeran, 2012 Summary checked; full text not yet About this exerciseThis exercise hasn't been tested itself. The game and its timing match the picture exercise exactly, so the two can be compared fairly. The planning step at the end uses the same method as “Plan your first step”. LimitsHow long any effect of a break or distraction lasts is unknown.A game on its own isn't expected to make starting easier. Sources Webb, Miles & Sheeran, 2012. Dealing with feeling: A meta-analysis of the effectiveness of strategies derived from the process model of emotion regulation. Psychological Bulletin, 138(4), 775–808 (opens in a new tab) (summary checked; full text not yet)BeginBack

You can stop at any time.Why this exercise?The science behind it: Implementation intentions What you doYou write down what you want to start, when you'll start, a tiny first step, and what you'll do if something gets in the way. Then you read your plan twice. The method: If-then planning (implementation intentions)Instead of only deciding what you want to do, you link a specific moment to a specific action: “When it's 7 pm and I'm at my desk, I'll open chapter 3.” The idea is that the moment itself then prompts you, so starting needs less deciding on the spot. What research says about this methodResearch found that people who made if-then plans reached their goals more often than people who only set the goal, across 94 experiments. Gollwitzer & Sheeran, 2006 Full text checkedA larger review of 642 experiments found that, after allowing for experiments that were never published, the benefit is small. It was larger when people strongly wanted the goal, and close to zero when they didn't. Sheeran, Listrom & Gollwitzer, 2025 Full text checked About this exerciseThis exercise follows the if-then planning method, but this version hasn't been tested itself. The research above tested if-then plans in its own forms and settings, not in this app. LimitsExpect a small effect at most, and only for goals you genuinely want.Effects were smaller online and in everyday settings than in the lab. Sources Gollwitzer & Sheeran, 2006. Implementation intentions and goal achievement: A meta-analysis of effects and processes.
